proof_paragraphs.new:
1.2 Retarded-field integrals. Put $C_a:=\overline B_a=\{y:|y|\le a\}$. If $|z|>a$, the ball of radius $(|z|-a)/2$ around $z$ is disjoint from $C_a$: the triangle inequality gives $|y|\ge|z|-|y-z|>a$ on that ball. Thus $C_a$ is closed. Also $C_a\subset B_{2a}$ since $a>0$, so it is bounded and hence compact by [F11]. A closed set is Borel, because its complement is open and the Borel sigma-algebra is closed under complements; under [A1], [F11] therefore makes $C_a$ Lebesgue measurable. The open ball $B_{2a}$ is measurable and has finite measure by [F7]. Applying measure monotonicity [F11] to $C_a\subset B_{2a}$ gives $\lambda_3(C_a)\le\lambda_3(B_{2a})<\infty$. These are exactly the compactness, measurability and finite-measure hypotheses needed for the set form of [F4]. Since $ho,J$ are jointly smooth and vanish for $|y|>a$, their values and their time derivatives vanish on $\partial B_a$; hence the potential integrals and the integrals obtained by one $x$- or $t$-derivative have the same values over $B_a$ and $\overline B_a$. proof_paragraphs.old: 1.3 Differentiation of the retarded current moment. Choose a bounded open interval $U$ containing $K$ and a compact interval $K_0$ whose interior contains $U$. Since $J$ and $J_t$ vanish on $\partial B_a$ by the smooth spatial-support hypothesis, the integral over $B_a$ agrees with that over the compact measurable finite-measure set $\overline B_a$ [F7]. For fixed $n\in S^2$, the map $(y,u)\mapsto J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)$ and its $u$ derivative $J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)$ are continuous on a neighborhood of $\overline B_a\times K_0$. Apply the set form of [F4] separately to each of the three vector components with integration set $\overline B_a$ and parameter $u$. Thus $\partial_u I(n,u)=\int_{B_a}J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy$ for every $u\in U$, so the definition of $V$ in the Statement is well-defined on a neighborhood of $K$. [given, F1, F4, F7, algebra, A1]

facts_added: [F11] A closed bounded subset of Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$ is compact; the Borel sigma-algebra contains open sets and their complements, and under Countable Choice every Borel subset is Lebesgue measurable, in particular every closed set. For a measure $\mu$ and measurable $A\subseteq B$, one has $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$. ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]] (2), [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]], [[prop-measure-monotonicity]])

proof_paragraphs.old: 1.1 Dipole moment identities. For each $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ put $p_i(u)=\int_{B_a}y_i\rho(y,u)\,dy$. Smoothness and vanishing of $\rho,J$ for $|y|>a$ imply that $\rho$, $J_i$ and their time derivatives vanish on $\partial B_a$. Thus the integrals of $y_i\rho$ and $y_i\rho_t$ over $B_a$ agree with those over the compact measurable finite-measure set $\overline B_a$ [F7]. Apply the set form of [F3] with integration set $\overline B_a$ and parameter $u$ to $f_i(y,u)=y_i\rho(y,u)$; its parameter derivative is $y_i\rho_t(y,u)$, and both are continuous on a neighborhood of $\overline B_a$ times any compact time interval. This gives $p_i'(u)=\int_{B_a}y_i\rho_t(y,u)\,dy$. Fix $R_0>a$ and apply the divergence theorem to $y\mapsto y_iJ(y,u)$ on $B_{R_0}$. The boundary flux is zero because $J=0$ near $\partial B_{R_0}$, while $\operatorname{div}(y_iJ)=J_i+y_i\operatorname{div}J$. Using $\rho_t=-\operatorname{div}J$ and the vanishing of the source outside $B_a$ gives $p_i'(u)=\int_{B_a}J_i(y,u)\,dy$. For each $i$, the integrals of $J_i$ and $J_{i,t}$ over $B_a$ agree with those over $\overline B_a$; the closed ball is compact measurable of finite measure by [F7]. Both integrands are continuous on a neighborhood of $\overline B_a$ times any compact time interval. Apply the set form of [F3] on $\overline B_a$ separately to each component $J_i$ with parameter $u$; differentiating the preceding identity gives $p_i''(u)=\int_{B_a}J_{i,t}(y,u)\,dy$. Collecting the three component identities yields $p''(u)=\int_{B_a}J_t(y,u)\,dy$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F7, algebra, A1]
proof_paragraphs.new: 1.1 Dipole moment identities. Thus it is an admissible fixed integration set for [F3]. For each $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ put $p_i(u)=\int_{B_a}y_i\rho(y,u)\,dy$. Smoothness and vanishing of $\rho,J$ for $|y|>a$ imply that $\rho$, $J_i$ and their time derivatives vanish on $\partial B_a$. Thus the integrals of $y_i\rho$ and $y_i\rho_t$ over $B_a$ agree with those over that compact measurable finite-measure set $\overline B_a$. Apply the set form of [F3] with integration set $\overline B_a$ and parameter $u$ to $f_i(y,u)=y_i\rho(y,u)$; its parameter derivative is $y_i\rho_t(y,u)$, and both are continuous on a neighborhood of $\overline B_a$ times any compact time interval. Using $\rho_t=-\operatorname{div}J$ and the vanishing of the source outside $B_a$ gives $p_i'(u)=\int_{B_a}J_i(y,u)\,dy$. For each $i$, the integrals of $J_i$ and $J_{i,t}$ over $B_a$ agree with those over $\overline B_a$; the closed ball has the compactness, measurability and finite measure just verified using [F1].
